subtitle: An independent review of how the website performs for a first-time, full-fee patient — what it does well, and where attention is lost before a booking is made.
summary: Two decisions here are better than almost anything else in this market. The logo reads “hēla medical | Drysdale MD” — a named physician, carried permanently on every page rather than buried on an About page. And the top of the site offers “Book now! TEXT (202) 333-4445”, which serves the patient who will not telephone a stranger but will happily send a message.

The first screen then works against both. The headline runs off the right edge of a phone: “DC'S BEST AWAR…”, “MEDICAL AESTHETIC…”, “established,…” — every line clipped. The hero itself is a stock photograph of the Washington skyline rather than the practice, the team or a result. And the only contact route sits inside a banner with a close button, so a visitor who dismisses it has no way to make contact from the first screen at all.

Evidence limitation: this review covers the homepage on mobile plus publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed, so the score is normalised across the six categories that were. Nothing here uses private analytics, and no traffic or revenue figures have been estimated.
scoreNote: Normalised across six assessed categories (90 points available). Treatment content and technical performance were not reviewed and are excluded rather than guessed. The trust and contact decisions here are unusually good — the score reflects how much of that the first screen gives away.

scorecard.finding: Every headline line is cut off at the right edge.
A physician named in the logo — with no detail beside the decision.
Text-to-book is excellent; it lives in a dismissible banner.
The hero shows a city, not the practice or its work.
Headline overflow across all three lines.
Full address including floor, plus a contact number.

strengthsLead: Two of these are decisions we spend most reports recommending. They are already made here.

strengths.title: The physician is named in the logo.
strengths.body: “hēla medical | Drysdale MD” appears in the masthead, so the doctor's name travels with every page rather than living on an About page most visitors never reach. Very few practices commit to this, and it answers the question that decides an injectables booking before it is asked.

strengths.title: Booking by text message.
strengths.body: “Book now! TEXT (202) 333-4445”. A large share of aesthetic enquiries begin with someone who wants to ask about suitability or price without committing to a conversation. Offering text meets them where they are.

strengths.title: The address is complete, down to the floor.
strengths.body: “3128 M Street NW, 3rd Floor, Washington DC 20007”. Precise enough to find without a second search, which matters more in a city than most practices allow for.

strengths.title: The new location is announced clearly.
strengths.body: Telling existing patients about a move before they arrive at the wrong address is a small courtesy that says the practice thinks about the people already on its books.

captionDesktop: The homepage carries the physician's name in the logo and a text-to-book number in the top banner.
captionMobile: Mobile, 390×844. The headline is clipped at the right edge on every line, and the hero is a stock photograph of the Washington skyline.

findings.heading: The headline runs off the side of the screen.
findings.evidence: At 390×844 the hero reads “DC'S BEST AWAR”, “MEDICAL AESTHETIC” and “established,” — each line cut at the right margin, with words truncated mid-spelling.
findings.why: The largest text on the page is unreadable on the device most patients use. Whatever claim the practice is making, a phone visitor cannot finish reading it — and an incomplete word reads as a site nobody has checked.
findings.recommended: Reduce the headline size at phone widths so the text wraps inside the viewport. One mobile styling rule usually corrects all three lines at once.

findings.heading: The only contact route can be closed.
findings.evidence: “Book now! TEXT (202) 333-4445” appears inside the top announcement banner, which carries a × close control. No booking button or telephone number appears elsewhere on the first screen.
findings.why: Banners get dismissed — often reflexively, before being read. A visitor who closes it is left on a first screen with no way to make contact at all, and the practice's best conversion idea disappears with it.
findings.recommended: Keep the text-to-book offer in the banner, and also place a permanent booking button and tap-to-call number in the header where they cannot be dismissed.

findings.heading: The hero is a city, not the practice.
findings.evidence: The hero occupies the full first screen with a stock photograph of the Washington skyline at dusk. No practitioner, premises, treatment or patient appears.
findings.why: A patient deciding where to have injectables is looking for evidence about this practice, and a skyline tells them only which city they are in — which they already knew. It is also imagery any competitor in DC could use tomorrow.
findings.recommended: Show Dr. Drysdale, the treatment rooms, or genuine before-and-after work. Given the physician's name is already in the logo, a photograph of him would compound a signal the practice is already committed to.

findings.heading: “DC's Best Award…” does not say which award.
findings.evidence: The visible portion of the headline reads “DC'S BEST AWAR…” before the text is cut off. No awarding body or year appears on the first screen.
findings.why: An unnamed award reads as a turn of phrase rather than a fact, so it persuades no more than any adjective — and combined with “best” it becomes a claim the visitor cannot check at all. Named, it becomes evidence.
findings.recommended: Name the award, the body and the year, and let it sit beside Dr. Drysdale's credential rather than in place of it.

findings.heading: The doctor is named but not introduced.
findings.evidence: “Drysdale MD” appears in the logo. No photograph, specialism, years in practice, or patient rating appears on the first screen.
findings.why: The name alone is already ahead of most practices. What it does not yet give a patient is a face and a reason — the details that turn recognition into confidence at the moment of booking.
findings.recommended: Add a photograph and one line of credential beneath the hero, and a rating with its review count beside the booking action.

psychology.plain: People expect a site to behave like the others they use.
psychology.site: Layout follows convention; the unfamiliar part is a first screen with no visible way to act once the banner is closed.

psychology.plain: Important actions should be big and easy to thumb.
psychology.site: The text number is a tappable link, which is right — but it sits in the element most likely to be dismissed.

psychology.plain: Reassurance has to sit where the doubt is.
psychology.site: No rating, review or credential detail appears near the booking route.
Strong in principle — a physician in the logo — but without a face or a specialism it stays a name rather than a person.
Clear while the banner is open, and absent the moment it is closed.

psychology.plain: Sensible pre-selections that serve the patient.
psychology.site: Offering text as the first contact method is a genuinely helpful default for a nervous first-time enquirer.

psychology.plain: Balanced, realistic communication is trusted more than perfection.
psychology.site: “Drysdale MD” is the most credible thing on the page. “DC's best” is the least, and they sit within inches of each other.

roadmap.actions: Fix the headline overflow at phone widths. Add a permanent booking button and tap-to-call number to the header so contact survives the banner being closed. Name the award.
Add Dr. Drysdale's photograph and credential beneath the hero. Replace the skyline with the practice, the team or real results. Add a rating and review count beside the booking action.

Build authority content around the physician — it is the practice's clearest differentiator. Treatment-page depth with candidacy notes. Post-treatment review requests. Begin measuring enquiry-to-booking so the calculator figures above become yours.

limitations: This review assessed the homepage at 390 pixels wide together with publicly visible information. Treatment-page depth and technical performance were not assessed and are excluded from the score rather than estimated; the total is normalised across the six categories reviewed (90 points available). Announcement banners behave differently for returning visitors who have already dismissed them.
